articles.title: Lego sales rise as World Cup and F1 ranges prove to be winners
articles.summary: Danish toymaker also scores success with KPop Demon Hunters, Star Wars and botanicals products. Business live – latest updates. body: The Danish toymaker said its revenues increased by 21% to 41.9bn Danish kroner (£4.8bn) in the first six months of 2026, driven by strong growth in the Americas, Europe and the Asia Pacific regions. Sales by its clients to consumers rose by 22%.
Net profit increased 32% to 8.6bn Danish kroner (£1bn) as the group launched 330 new products including its high-tech Smart Play kit, with bricks that emit sounds and light.

Niels B Christiansen, the chief executive of Lego Group, said: “We are very pleased with our strong start to 2026 and the excitement we see for the Lego brand. Our portfolio of products offers something for everyone, and culturally relevant brand experiences continue to drive demand across the globe. Our success in the market means we can maintain high investment levels in growth and sustainability for both the short and long term.”

articles.title: Freddie Mercury’s ‘splendid things’ to go on display at V&A
articles.summary: Eight costumes spanning Queen frontman’s career will feature in a free trail developed with his former fiancee. Eight famous costumes worn by Freddie Mercury, including the outfit featured on the cover of Queen’s debut album and the catsuit from the video for Bohemian Rhapsody, are to go on display…
body: Freddie Mercury | Splendid Things, a free trail developed with Mercury’s former fiancee and close friend Mary Austin, will run from 24 October 2026 to 17 January 2027. Austin is lending seven of the looks, which span Mercury’s career from the 1970s to his final years.

Among them is a monochrome ensemble worn for an early Queen gig at Imperial College and pictured on the cover of the band’s eponymous debut album. Also on display will be the “Mercury Wing” catsuit, designed by Wendy de Smet and worn during the A Night at the Opera tour in 1975-76, as well as in the groundbreaking Bohemian Rhapsody video.

Mercury’s crown and cloak, designed by Diana Moseley and worn during Queen’s 1986 Magic Tour, will also feature. He wore the outfit for the band’s final live performance at Knebworth that year. The display will also include a costume from the Made in Heaven music video, as well as accessories and items from his personal wardrobe.
The trail takes its name from a remark Mercury made in 1978: “I like to be surrounded by splendid things. I want to lead a Victorian life surrounded by exquisite clutter.”
points: Eight costumes spanning Queen frontman’s career will feature in a free trail developed with his former fiancee.

From venture capital investments and startup launches to product drops and regulatory updates, we’ll make sure you never miss a beat when it comes to the AI news that matters.
The news: Amazon faces lawsuit over training AI models on video content from Twitch.

Why it matters: The class action lawsuit against Amazon has been brought on behalf of millions of Twitch streamers who allege the platform’s parent company, Amazon, used their content to train AI without permission or compensation. According to the BBC, reportedly 215 million hours of content was generated via the platform in the first few months of 2026 alone. While the use of these videos was only announced in August, allowing people to then opt-out of having their data used this way, it is unclear how long Amazon was harnessing this content.

articles.title: Inside Tennis’s Booming Influencer Economy
articles.summary: As Grand Slams become increasingly valuable stages for the creator economy, brands and tournaments are racing to capitalize on the attention without diluting what made the events desirable in the first place.
body: When the US Open begins in New York later this month, amid the bustling crowds, sponsor pop-ups and iconic Manhattan food outposts, there will be a new content machine operating in the background. Creators will film their outfits, review the food and give followers a look inside brand experiences and premium seats, broadcasting the spectacle of being at the Open to millions of people beyond the gates. Brands are spending tens — and in some cases hundreds — of thousands of dollars to make sure they have a place in that content.

During the US Open, influencer management company DBA consistently sees three to four times more brand interest and partnership opportunities for its tennis-adjacent talent than at other tennis events, according to vice president of talent Kirstin MacGowan. “Brands are increasingly investing in culturally relevant sporting moments,” she says, “and the US Open’s relevance extends well beyond tennis.”

articles.title: Back to School: How are Parents Shopping for Gen Alpha?
articles.summary: Despite tight budgets, parent spending for kids remains stable. The key for brands will be adapting to a new, increasingly fashion-literate generation of youngsters who know what they want.
body: Parents these days have a lot on their plate, not least an increasingly digitized, discerning set of kids fast approaching term time. The issue at hand? Fashion matters for school-age children (5-18) more than ever, but the economic climate is testing parents’ wallets.

Some context: US inflation hit 4.2% in May, per the Bureau of Labor Statistics. According to a recent survey published by Deloitte, consumer sentiment remains shaky, with 57% of Americans expecting the economy to worsen in the next six months — the highest figure the company has reported since 2020.

For retailers and brands wanting to tap in, differentiation will rely on newness and innovation. “The back-to-school season is the second biggest time period of retail sales each year, behind Christmas, and so far, the results have been encouraging,” says Dana Telsey, CEO of Telsey Advisory Group. Indeed, while the expected budget per child remains flat at $557, Deloitte values the US back-to-school market at $30.4 billion. Promotions for value-driven parents remain key, but the approach — and retail offering — require some fine-tuning.
points: Despite tight budgets, parent spending for kids remains stable.

articles.title: Should Brands Be Patrons of Art and Culture?
articles.summary: Brands are beginning to rethink their role in culture, moving from trying to create or control it to funding the people and the ecosystems already producing it.
body: For years, brands have worked to both feed into and embed themselves in culture. But as audiences tire of branded content where the sales pitch overshadows the creativity, and the commercial machinery of marketing becomes harder to ignore, some brands are reconsidering their roles. Instead of trying to create culture themselves, they’re helping to fund the conditions upon which others do so.

Once upon a time, Procter & Gamble sponsored daytime dramas such as Ma Perkins, becoming so synonymous with the genre they eventually became known as “soap operas”; the Grand Ole Opry started out simply as a radio program sponsored by an insurance company, before becoming one of the defining institutions of American country music; the Tour de France came from French newspaper L’Équipe; and the Michelin Guide — including its coveted stars — was created by Michelin tyres.

Despite these past wins, a new generation of brands and platforms is beginning to rethink what it means to participate in culture, moving beyond contracted deliverables and multiple rounds of sign-offs toward models that put more money, access and resources behind the people making it.

articles.title: In Japan's Niigata Prefecture, the Ancient Culinary Tradition of Fermentation Is Very Much Alive
articles.summary: From prized sake to pickled potato salad and snow-aged ham, here's how to sip and savor your way through a part of the country known for its fermented foods.
body: My first stop was Willow House, a café and bakery where washi lanterns cast gentle light onto the natural-wood interiors and jazz seeps from the speakers. It's part of the Suzu Group, a coterie of restaurants, izakayas, and guesthouses that have put a modern spin on Niigata's ancient culinary craft. The bakery churns out a rotation of sourdough breads, caramelized apple rolls, and gratin toast with dashi-infused béchamel, while the café has a snack menu featuring miso pickled potato salad, fermented summer tomato salsa, and snow-aged ham.

I continued the tour with a skewer of rice dumplings coated in a sticky-sweet fermented soy sauce glaze at the takeaway counter of Eguchi Dango, a historic fourth-generation wagashi sweets shop. Next is a visit to the Settaya 6th Avenue Fermentation Museum Komegura, located in the former warehouse of a “saffron sake” brewery. Its exterior is decorated with colorful Chinese zodiac panels, while inside is a lab with exhibits on fermentation and a café. Its gift shop sells miso; amazake, a nutritious rice-and-koji drink known for its alleged longevity benefits; and bottles of saffron liqueur made from a recipe that was patented in 1884.
